title: Wood's background, Army service and early exposure to jazz
summary: Born in Richmond in 1928, drafted in 1951, taught at Tulane and JMU; recalls Lead Belly records, Mister Jelly Roll, and meeting drummer Paul Barbarin at his first parade.

story.theme_name: Drafted: musicians in the military and the war years
story.community_name: Drafted: service bands, USO shows and the war years

blocks.x: All right. So, tell me a little bit about yourself. Where were you born?

I was born in Richmond, Virginia in 1928, and with the exception of the years that I spent in New Orleans as a graduate student in the late 1950s, I've lived in Virginia almost all of my life. I was in the Army for a while, but other than that, I am a lifelong resident of Virginia. I'm on the faculty of James Madison University in the past five summers. This being the fifth, I have come and taught summer school in the History Department at Tulane, from which institution I graduated with an MA and PhD degree that I earned back in the 50s.
Well, where were you in the service, just out of curiosity?

Out of curiosity, I was drafted in 51 and assigned to an Alabama-Mississippi National Guard division that had been called a federal service. I spent a year in South Carolina with them and another year in Indiana, and then I was released and went back home.
Well, did you hear a lot of jazz in those places, like Virginia and Indiana?

No, no, no, Richard. No? No? I didn't hear much jazz in any of those places. I guess before I came here as a graduate student, I had, as a high school student, I had enjoyed listening to a great variety of music. I had particularly enjoyed some black folk blues people, Lead Belly. I had a great collection of Lead Belly records when I was a high school student. And some Josh White records that I played a lot, Blind Lemon Jefferson records. And I had read a book or two. I can't really even tell you. It was a book that was published, I don't know, I guess the late 40s, called Mr. Jelly Roll. Alan Lomax did it. Yes. I read that book before I came down here. So I had this, you know, just a young man's awareness of the music. But when I came down here, you introduced me to it in a more direct way and I came to enjoy it very much. I remember that one of the first brass band street parades that I attended that you told me about, and I think we went together, my wife then and some other Tulane people. And as we had assembled in front of the neighborhood grocery store where the band was sort of coming together and all these people were standing around, you pointed out and then introduced me to the man who was a drummer of this particular band and his name was Paul Barberin. And I was just dumbfounded because I had, you know, that name was one that I had remembered from reading about as having been somebody who had been a New Orleans musician who had played with bands in Chicago in the 20s and so on. And then there he was standing on the street corner in New Orleans in 1955 or something. It was just quite a surprise to me. And so I used, you know, I came to enjoy very much going to hear the brass bands play whenever we had the chance to go and hear them play. And in 55, 6, 7, 8 in there, there were more chances. There were a fair number of chances. I think back on it, maybe there weren't as many as I sort of thought there were then. But it seemed to me that in the summertime where you could go to a parade practically every weekend.
